chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Numbers That Drive Value

lessons.title: Risk and the Cost of Capital in Plain Language

children.text: Ask a finance team why a project was rejected and you will often hear that it "did not clear the hurdle rate". Ask what the hurdle rate is and where it came from, and the room goes quiet. This lesson answers that question without a single Greek letter you cannot explain to a colleague over chai.

body.text: The discount rate is not a technicality buried in a spreadsheet. It is the return investors could earn elsewhere at the same risk. Every rupee your business earns has to beat that, or the money should have gone elsewhere.

children.text: Why a Discount Rate Exists at All

Two reasons, and both are ordinary. The first is time: ₹100 today can sit in a bank or a government bond and become more than ₹100 next year, so a rupee promised later is worth less than one held now. The second is risk: a promised rupee from a profitable listed company is more believable than one from a two year old startup, so the startup has to promise more to attract the same money.
The starting point is the
risk-free rate
, the return you can earn without taking business risk. In India that means government securities.

markDefs.definition: The return available with effectively no default risk. In Indian valuations this is normally the yield on a long-dated government security, usually the 10 year G-sec.

stats.label: RBI repo rate
stats.context: Unchanged through several meetings up to September 2026

body.text: Note which number valuers use. Not the repo rate, which is an overnight policy rate, but the yield on a long-dated government bond, because a business is being valued over many years. As at September 2026 that is roughly 7%. When rates move, every valuation in the country moves with them, even for companies whose operations have not changed at all.

children.text: The Cost of Equity: What Shareholders Demand

Shareholders are paid last and can lose everything, so they demand more than the government pays. The standard model adds a premium for equity risk, scaled by how volatile this particular business is against the market.

body.caption: The Capital Asset Pricing Model, the starting point in almost every Indian valuation report
The three inputs, with Indian values as at September 2026

cells: The extra return investors demand for holding equities rather than government bonds
Damodaran's July 2026 country data puts India at about 7.31%, against about 4.17% for mature markets
How much this business's returns swing relative to the market. 1.0 means it moves with the market
Estimated from listed peers, adjusted for the company's own debt level

children.text: Put them together for a business whose beta is 1.2, meaning it swings about 20% more than the market. Cost of equity = 7.0% + (1.2 × 7.3%) = about 15.8%. That is the return an equity investor expects, and therefore the bar the business has to clear.

body.title: Compute a cost of equity
body.prompt: Using a risk-free rate of 7.0% and an equity risk premium of 7.3%, what is the cost of equity for a company with a beta of 1.5? Give your answer as a percentage.
body.explanation: 7.0% + (1.5 × 7.3%) = 7.0% + 10.95% = 17.95%. A steel or real estate company that swings hard with the economy will sit here. A defensive business with a beta of 0.7 would need only 7.0% + 5.11% = about 12.1%, and would therefore be worth more for the same cash flows.

body.text: Beta is the most abused input in Indian valuation reports. Private companies have no traded share price, so beta is borrowed from listed peers and then adjusted for the target's own debt. If a report gives you a beta without saying which peers it came from, ask.

children.text: The Cost of Debt: Cheaper, and Not Only Because of the Rate
Lenders rank ahead of shareholders and usually hold security, so they accept less. Debt has a second advantage: interest is deductible before tax, so the government funds part of the cost.

body.caption: At a 25.17% effective corporate tax rate, a 10% loan costs the company about 7.48%

body.title: Why the tax shield is real money

children.text: Take a company with EBIT of ₹100 crore, taxed at about 25%.
With no debt: tax is charged on ₹100 crore, so roughly ₹25 crore goes to the government
With ₹10 crore of interest: tax is charged on ₹90 crore, so roughly ₹22.5 crore goes to the government
The ₹10 crore of interest cost the company only about ₹7.5 crore after the tax saved
That is why cost of debt is always used after tax in a WACC, while cost of equity is not. Dividends are paid out of post-tax profit and save the company nothing.

content.text: The tax shield is only worth something if the company is actually paying tax. A loss-making company gets no benefit, so using an after-tax cost of debt for it overstates the advantage of borrowing.

children.text: Putting Both Together: WACC
Most companies use a mix of both, so the discount rate is a weighted average of the two, weighted by how much of the capital each provides. This is the
weighted average cost of capital
, or WACC.

markDefs.definition: The blended return a company must earn to satisfy both lenders and shareholders, weighted by the proportion of debt and equity in its capital. Written as WACC.

body.caption: E is equity, D is debt, Ke the cost of equity and Kd the pre-tax cost of debt

children.text: Take Nandi Logistics from Chapter 1. It is funded 60% by equity and 40% by debt. Its cost of equity works out to 15.8% and it borrows at 10%, which after tax is about 7.5%.

body.title: Change the mix
body.prompt: Nandi repays part of its loans. The capital structure becomes 70% equity and 30% debt, with the cost of equity still 15.8% and the after-tax cost of debt still 7.5%. What is the new WACC, as a percentage?
body.explanation: (0.70 × 15.8%) + (0.30 × 7.5%) = 11.06% + 2.25% = about 13.3%. Less debt means a higher WACC on this arithmetic, because debt is the cheaper source. In the real world that is not the end of the story: more debt raises the risk of financial distress, which pushes up both the cost of equity and the rate lenders charge. There is a sensible middle, not a rule that says borrow as much as possible.

children.text: Small Changes in the Rate, Large Changes in the Value
This is why the discount rate is worth arguing about. Take a business generating ₹100 crore of free cash flow next year, growing at 5% a year forever, and change only the discount rate.

body.title: Value of the same ₹100 crore of cash flow at different discount rates

body.text: A 1.5 percentage point change in the discount rate moved the value by about ₹334 crore, a fifth of the company, without anyone touching a single business assumption. When a buyer and a seller are far apart on price, the disagreement is often about risk, not about the business plan.

children.text: Why Private Companies Face a Higher Rate
A CAPM number built from listed peers understates the risk of a smaller unlisted company. Valuers add further premiums, and these are matters of judgment that must be explained in the report.

body.title: Listed large cap versus small private company

columns.label: Listed large company
points: Beta observable from its own traded price
Audited quarterly results and continuous disclosure
Shares can be sold on NSE or BSE on any trading day
Cost of equity often lands in the low to mid teens

columns.label: Small private company
points: Beta borrowed from peers and adjusted
Often one plant, a handful of customers and one promoter who is the business
Annual audited accounts, limited disclosure between them
No market to sell into, so investors demand compensation for being locked in
Cost of equity commonly needs a size and company-specific premium on top

children.text: Add a combined size and company-specific premium of, say, 5% to the earlier 15.8% and the cost of equity becomes about 20.8%. That is not a punishment. It is the honest price of concentration risk, key person risk and illiquidity.

body.title: The hurdle rate argument
body.question: A division head argues that a project should be approved because it returns 11%, and the company can borrow at 9%. The company's WACC is 13%. What is wrong with the argument?
options: Nothing, since 11% beats the 9% borrowing cost
The project must clear the blended cost of all the capital the company uses, which is 13%, not just the rate on one source of funding
The project should be compared against the repo rate of 5.25%
The comparison should be against inflation, so 11% is comfortably fine
body.explanation: Funding one project with a specific loan does not make that loan's rate the right hurdle. The company's capital is a pool of debt and equity, and shareholders are also funding the project. At a WACC of 13%, an 11% project destroys about 2% of value a year on the money invested. This is one of the most common and most expensive mistakes in Indian corporate capital allocation.

body.title: One hurdle rate for every division
body.scenario: You sit on the investment committee of a diversified group. The CFO applies a single 15% hurdle rate to every proposal: a new cement plant, a software subsidiary, and a stable warehousing business with 10 year leases to listed tenants. The software business complains that it never gets funded. The warehousing team gets approvals easily and keeps proposing more projects.
body.prompt: What is going wrong, and what would you propose?
body.modelAnswer:
1. A single rate ignores that risk differs by business. Warehousing with long leases to strong tenants is far less risky than a software venture, so both being tested at 15% is neither fair nor economically sound.
2. The predictable consequence is exactly what is happening. Low-risk projects clear an artificially high bar and get funded generously, while genuinely valuable higher-risk projects are rejected. Over time the group drifts towards low-return, low-risk activity.
3. The fix is division-level discount rates, each built from the betas and capital structures of listed companies in that sector, not from the group average.
4. Warehousing should face a lower rate, and probably a more demanding size of investment, while software should face a higher rate but be allowed to compete on its own terms.
5. Whatever rates are chosen, write down the inputs: risk-free rate, equity risk premium, beta source, and any size premium. A rate nobody can explain becomes a political instrument rather than an economic test.
6. Revisit the rates when government bond yields move materially. A WACC set when the 10 year G-sec was at 6% is stale when it is at 7%.

body.title: The right benchmark
body.textWithBlank: In Indian valuations the risk-free rate is normally taken from the yield on a 10 year ___ security rather than from the RBI repo rate.
body.explanation: The repo rate is an overnight policy rate. A business is valued over many years, so the benchmark should have a comparable horizon, which is why the 10 year government security yield is used.

body.title: Interrogate any discount rate in one minute
steps: What risk-free rate was used, and as at what date?
What equity risk premium, and from which published source?
Where did beta come from: which listed peers, and was it adjusted for debt?
Were size or company-specific premiums added, and what justifies their size?
What capital structure weights were used, and are they the company's actual mix or a target?
Is the cost of debt after tax, and is the company actually paying tax?
Does the rate match the cash flows: rupee cash flows need a rupee discount rate

body.label: Damodaran: country default spreads and risk premiums
body.description: The equity risk premium table most Indian valuation reports cite for India. Check the date on the file you are reading, since it is updated periodically and every report should say which vintage it used.

cards.definition: The return available without default risk, taken in India from the 10 year G-sec yield.
The extra return investors demand for holding equities instead of government bonds.
How much a business's returns move relative to the overall market. Above 1 means more volatile.
Risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium, plus any size or company-specific premium.
The interest rate on borrowings, used after tax because interest is deductible.
The blended cost of debt and equity, weighted by how much of each funds the business.
The minimum return a project must earn to be worth doing. It should be built from the WACC of that kind of business.

points: A discount rate exists for two plain reasons: time and risk. It is the return available elsewhere at the same risk.
In India the risk-free rate comes from the 10 year G-sec, about 7.0% as at September 2026, not from the 5.25% repo rate.
Cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium. At an India equity risk premium of about 7.3% and a beta of 1.2, that is about 15.8%.
Debt is cheaper both because lenders rank ahead of shareholders and because interest is tax deductible, making a 10% loan cost about 7.5% after tax.
WACC blends the two by their weights. At 60% equity and 40% debt, this lesson's example came to about 12.5%.
Value is highly sensitive to the rate: moving from 11% to 14% cut the example business from about ₹1,667 crore to about ₹1,111 crore.
Private companies carry size and company-specific premiums on top, and a single group-wide hurdle rate quietly starves the riskier businesses of capital.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Market rates quoted are as at September 2026 and change constantly, so always use current figures in live work. Nandi Logistics is fictional. The equity risk premium cited is one widely used published estimate, not an official figure, and reasonable valuers differ on it.
